newsitem.title: RUSSIA: No quick fix seen to Russia tax problems - analysts.
newsitem.headline: No quick fix seen to Russia tax problems - analysts.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund, dismayed over low tax revenues, wants proof Russia can rake in extra cash before it hands over part of a $10 billion loan, but analysts said on Friday that no quick fix was in sight.
An IMF mission monitoring Russia's economic performance left without deciding whether to recommend paying the latest $330 million monthly tranche, holding up payment for a second time.
The IMF team will return for more talks next month but Finance Minister Alexander Livshits acknowledged on Friday that Russia could face problems unless revenues improved.
"Problems with IMF tranches may arise in November unless there is a positive dynamic in budget revenues," he was quoted as saying by Prime-Tass news agency.

Tax evasion is unacceptably high in Russia and the government, short of tax receipts, has left many bills unpaid. Workers across Russia have not been paid for months, taking cold comfort from sharply lower inflation rates.
The IMF delayed paying one tranche of its three-year loan in the summer because of concern over the budget and analysts said it would be hard for Russia to raise revenue rapidly.

"They will try to improve the situation, they will do whatever they can. Unfortunately I do not see any quick return from any operation at the moment," said Pavel Teplukhin, chief economist at Troika-Dialog.
The government has declared war on tax dodgers, setting up an emergency commission under Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and threatening to bankrupt firms with big tax debts.
"Revenue collection should be significantly improved in November and the IMF will come back and approve the payment," said Arkady Dvorkovich, of the finance ministry's economic expert group.
He said tax collection had improved in October over September, but revenues needed to double in November.

Tax collection was 74 percent of target in the first nine months of this year and the budget deficit is running at some six percent of gross domestic product, using the IMF methods of calculating the gap.
But the IMF, which has made tax collection a key criteria for loan payments, wants clear evidence of credible and sustainable improvements in revenue.
"They do not believe any more in promises, they want to see actual figures," Dvorkovich said.

If the IMF does not pay the October tranche, Russia could be forced to borrow more on domestic debt markets, pushing yields up again. If yields stay high, the government will have extra problems financing the deficit.
The alternative -- slashing spending from current low levels -- could trigger social unrest.
Defence Minister Igor Rodionov warned on Friday that the army already needed extra cash.

"Russia's leadership and society should know that the chronic lack of funds is taking the armed forces to the brink of undesirable, and even uncontrollable, developments," Interfax news agency quoted him as saying.

The delay to the IMF follows on the heels of Russia's better than expected credit rating and some analysts said it could raise the cost of the government's planned Eurobond issue, due around the time the IMF returns to continue its review.
Teplukhin said the IMF would pay more attention to government efforts than to results and would pay up. "It has become an issue of politics rather than economics."

However, James Fenkner, head of research at CentreInvest Securities, said the IMF was taking too narrow a view of the Russian economy. "They are looking at it as a check list, not as if it was an entire system," he said.
